description_block:
This composition reprises the central panel of a triptych that is now lost, whose wings depicted the Flight into Egypt and the Nativity, probably dating to 1518â1519. Originally attributed to Lucas van Leyden, then to Herri Met de Bles and finally to Rogier van der Weyden, FriedlÃ¤nder suggested the name of the Master of the Von Groote Adoration in 1915 and 1933, identifying the prototype as the panel in the Johnson collection, now in Philadelphia (inv. 383); in his opinion it served as the model for the triptych in Munich (Alte Pinakothek, inv. 1431 a-c). In 1978, Dan Ewing proposed that the works in Philadelphia and Munich shared a common prototype, now lost, which could be assigned to the artist Jan de Beer, with the Munich version as the most faithful.
Jan de Beerâs work was one of the first Antwerp compositions to have been widely copied; after this, works by Pieter Coecke van Aelst would follow suit: additional versions were at that time considered to be on a par with the original compositions and seen as a way of disseminating a work to a larger audience and making it accessible to more collectors and churches.
Dan Ewing has identified about fifty copies and variants of the Munich triptych â not an exhaustive list â making a distinction between those that reprise the whole triptych; those that only reproduce the central panel but which were probably originally part of a triptych; and lastly complete triptychs whose wings do not match any of the known compositions. The present Adoration of the Magi faithfully reproduces the Munich composition, with the exception of two shepherds on the extreme right. However,an infrared examination of our panel reveals that these were originally present in the underlying drawing, and were probably covered over in a relatively early restoration.
In 2016 (op. cit., p. 189), Dan Ewing pointed out the careful attention paid to the balance of the composition and the play of diagonals and vanishing lines, in his view reaching a degree of accuracy that the artist would never surpass. Ewing classified the present version as one of the first ten iterations on his list, partly because the design is so faithful to the central panel of the Munich triptych, but also because of the comparability of the details and palette.
The quality of the present Adoration of the Magi must have impressed distinguished collectors over the years. For a long time in the Chaix dâEst-Ange family, our painting featured in an article about the collection in the magazine Les Arts (see bibliography), alongside works by Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Murillo and Van Dyck.

description_block:
Cristoforo Roncalli was one of the most acclaimed and sought after late Mannerist painters in Rome at the turn of the seventeenth century. His altarpieces and fresco cycles are preserved in over twenty-seven different churches in Rome, as well as being represented in most of the major seicento collections of that city, including those of the Barberini, Borghese, Colonna, and the Spada. Works by Pomarancio are very rare on the market as most of his career was spent painting frescoes and altarpieces which are still in situ. 
Born in Pomarance, he completed his initial training fifty miles away in Florence, before moving to Siena in 1575, where he was commissioned to paint the altarpiece of Saint Anthony in the Duomo. He is recorded in Rome from 1582, where he achieved great commercial success, being one of only a handful of artists in the seventeenth century who were ever paid more than 750 scudi for an altarpiece.1 He was also held in very high esteem by his fellow artists, with Sir Peter Paul Rubens describing him in a letter to the Duke of Mantua in 1606 as being 'considered among the the top in Rome'.2 Perhaps the pinnacle of his career was his creation as a 'Cavaliere di Cristo' by Clement VIII in 1607 in recognition for his work in the Capella Clementina in St Peterâs, Rome. Dr Ian Kennedy, to whom we are grateful for endorsing the attribution to Roncalli, notes a Sienese influence in the present work and suggests an early date. The tenderness of the Virgin's features and her delicate luminosity are indeed reminiscent of Sienese painting and comparable to an early Madonna and Child in the Gallerie Nazionali delle Marche, Urbino, thought to have been executed during Roncalli's first few years in Rome.3 Parallels can also be drawn with the graceful fall of drapery, the blessing gesture of the Christ Child and the position of the Virgin's slender hands.  
1. R. Spear, Caravaggio Reflections and Refractions, Dorchester 2014, pp. 209â10. 2. Spear 2014, p. 199. 3. I. Chiappini di Sorio, Cristoforo Roncalli detto il Pomarancio, Bergamo 1983, pp. 130â31, cat. no. 66, reproduced.

description_block:
A clay pipe, a tobacco box and a brazier were the indispensable requisites for a seventeenth century Dutch smoker. Still lifes depicting this specific ensemble of objects, also called Toebackjes, grew in popularity from the 1620s, when tobacco was introduced into the United Provinces. Much of Johannes Frisâs work was devoted to them. Still a mysterious figure, this artist worked in Amsterdam between 1647 and 1672, specializing in still lifes. Materials and textures are reproduced in the finest detail, with a restrained palette of grey, ochre, white, terracotta and brown tones. These âtonalâ still lifes followed in the wake of Pieter Claeszâs work in the 1630s, though Fris was closer to Jan van de Velde the Younger in the arrangement of the objects and his manner of applying colour to the canvas (see for example Still Life with Stoneware Jug and Pipe, 1650, National Gallery of Art, Washington, inv. 2019.13.1).
The pipe, the tobacco box, the brazier, the Westerwald stoneware jug (decorated with the emblem of the city of Amsterdam) and the glass seem to be objects taken from the painterâs workshop: they appear in several of his works, for example the Still Life signed and dated 1650 in the Fondation Custodia, Paris, and in the Still Life signed and dated 1665, sold in our rooms (Sothebyâs, New York, 28 January 2021, lot 37). The tall beer glass, commonly called a pasglas, was used for drinking games and often depicted in debauched tavern scenes. The elements assembled in the painting suggest an evening of drinking and smoking among friends, but point out to a keen-eyed viewer the dangers of idleness and excess. The pasglas references the notion of measured temperance , while the broken brazier and the pipe may be associated with the concept of vanitas, underlining the fragility of human life, as ephemeral as a coil of smoke.

subject_matter: couple, tavern, woman, man, servant, dog, playing cards, stoneware pitcher, broken pipe, laughter
description_block:
It was in the increasingly Puritan context of the United Provinces of the Netherlands in the seventeenth century that the production of paintings of debauched scenes in taverns developed. Here, the couple in the centre seem to be involved in a struggle: while the woman is toppling from the table, the man is pulling her towards him and undoing her bodice. Although she seems to be in an awkward position, the servant woman gives a hint of a smile, as though to mock the drunkâs clumsiness. Playing cards, a stoneware pitcher and a broken pipe have been dragged of the slipping tablecloth and lie on the floor, emblems of the excesses taking place in the tavern. At their feet, a dog â symbol of marital fidelity â snarls as if in disapproval of their licentious behaviour. The footwarmer has lost the brazier that should be heating it, adding to the lewd tone of the scene taking place around it.
The remaining figures watch the situation with a mocking air. One of the men seated at the table suggestively stuffs tobacco in his pipe, while casting a mischievous eye at the viewer. The old woman, the matchmaker, claps her hands. At the window, three young women are jeering.
The humorous tone is typical of Netherlandish genre scenes in the Golden Age, but is also characteristic of Molenaerâs work. He trained in the 1630s in Frans Halsâs workshop in Haarlem, alongside Adriaen Brouwer and Adriaen van Ostade. He shared with these colleagues a taste for tavern scenes, joyous celebrations and weddings. Although he was capable of a very fine finish in his portraits, he applied a more supple brushstroke to subjects considered vulgar. The materiality of this touch resonates with the artistâs painted descriptions of the vices and temptations of the carnal sphere.

description_block:
The Portrait of Marie de MÃ©dicis painted by Van Dyck in 1631 (MusÃ©e des Beaux-Arts, Bordeaux, Inv. Bx E 3) shows a dignified seated woman, despite the difficulties the queen was experiencing at that time. After the failure of the âDay of the Dupesâ, on 10 November 1630, when her son Louis XIII chose Cardinal Richelieu over her, she went in exile in the Spanish Netherlands. In Van Dyckâs version, it is possible to see behind her the fortress of Het Steen and the tower of the cathedral in Antwerp, where she was staying in late 1631. A replica of this work, probably painted the same year, is in the MusÃ©e des Beaux-Arts in Lille (MusÃ©e des Beaux-Arts, Lille, inv. P. 58).
This portrait seems to be a reduced version of the original composition, reprising the clothes worn by Marie de MÃ©dicis and her confident expression against a dark background. She wears the same black silk dress with a wide white collar; only her jewellery is different: her black earrings and simple gold chain have been replaced with large white pearls, whose nacreous gleam illuminates the queenâs face. This parure is similar to the one worn by Marie de MÃ©dicis in the portrait painted by Frans Pourbus in 1613. It is possible that the present work was by the draughtsman and painter Daniel Dumonstier, a portraitist who was much admired by the French aristocracy in the seventeenth century.

description_block: This fascinating Allegory of Touch, still in fine condition, revisits an iconographic model devised by Jan Brueghel the Elder for his series The Five Senses, created in collaboration with Peter Paul Rubens and now in the Museo del Prado in Madrid (The Sense of Touch; Museo del Prado; inv. P001398). This series of paintings depicting the five senses is an excellent example of the art that was being produced in Antwerp in the early seventeenth century and was thence widely disseminated. Peter Paul Rubens and Jan Brueghel the Elder successfully collaborated to produce a series remarkable for its high quality and undeniable aesthetic appeal: it was reflected and circulated, with many variations, in works by numerous artists and their workshops throughout northern Europe. The present work has long been interpreted â incorrectly â either as an allegory of fire, because it illustrates a number of objects created with the help of fire, or as an allegory of discord. In reality, it is without doubt an allegory of touch, featuring many of the elements in the original work by Rubens and Brueghel. The depiction of the scene is characterized by its precise detail and the variety of figures, animals and objects it contains. Venus and Cupid are placed in the centre of the âgraveyard of weaponsâ, with Venus holding a bird in her left hand and indicating the brazier to Cupid with her right hand. Various symbolic elements are used to illustrate the sense of touch, such as animals (scorpions, lizards, snakes), objects (armour, battle-axes, swords, a bow and arrows) as well as the visual metaphor of Vulcanâs forge. It is interesting to observe that the work by Jan van Kessel, Venus at Vulcanâs Forge, in the Hermitage State Museum in St Petersburg (Inv. ÐÐ­-1709), displays significant similarities to the painting by Jan Bruegel the Younger and Hendrick van Balen. Architectural elements such as carvings in high relief, columns and ruins complete this representation of the allegory of touch. Another almost identical version of this work is in the MusÃ©e Calvet in Avignon (Inv. 827.5.24). This is considered to be by Hendrick van Balen (for the figures) and Jan Brueghel the Younger (for the landscape and still life elements) â see Klaus Ertz, Jan Brueghel d.J. (1601-1678), Freren, 1984, no. 227; and Bettina Werche, Hendrick van Balen (1575-1632): Ein Antwerper Kabinettbildmaler der Rubenszeit, Turnhout, 2004, vol. I no. A 184 p. 211; ill. vol. II p. 450. The Avignon painting seems to be of slightly higher quality than the present version, which was probably produced by the workshop; however, the main figures are sufficiently fine to suggest that as far as they are concerned Van Balen himself may have had a hand in their execution.

subject_matter: portrait, ducal cloak, cuirass, baton, military, cavalry clash, armor, symbols, orders, man
description_block:
In 1704, Duc Claude-Louis-Hector de Villars (1653â1734), thirty-ninth Marshal of France, commissioned a portrait of himself from Rigaud, at a time when his reputation was growing thanks to his military victories. His cloak embroidered with the Order of the Holy Spirit, which he received in 1705, suggests that the work was completed that same year. Now lost, it was displayed in the ChÃ¢teau de Vaux-le-Vicomte, which the duke had bought. A second version, similar to the 1704 work, was commissioned in 1713; here Villars is also wearing a Golden Fleece which the marshal had been awarded that same year. Many copies were made in different formats and on different supports.
The present portrait of the Duc de Villars is one of the copies of the second version with him wearing the Golden Fleece. The marshal had turned to a well-known artist to evoke his power and military genius in a three-quarter length portrait. Wearing a cuirass and with his sword sheathed, his gaze fixed on the horizon, he rests his right hand on his marshalâs baton, decorated with fleur-de-lys, while his left hand rests on his hip. He is clad in the ducal cloak of the Peers of France â an honour he had received in 1709 â lined in ermine and embroidered with the Cross of the Holy Spirit, as well as the blue riband of the Order of the Holy Spirit and the ribbon of the Golden Fleece. In the background, under a dark sky, a cavalry clash is taking place, perhaps the Battle of HÃ¶chstÃ¤dt. Playing on tones and contrasts to emphasize his attributes, Hyacinthe Rigaud highlights the distinctions of the man who would be known, at the end of his life, as âthe Sword of the Frenchâ.
While the composition recalls those of Louis XIV, King of France (1701, Madrid, Museo Nacional del Prado, inv. 2343) and Louis (1682â1712), Duc de Bourgogne (1702â1703, Versailles, MusÃ©e National du ChÃ¢teau, inv. 7539), the apparel and posture of the duke seem to have been devised especially for him and served as a model for many later portraits, as for instance Louis Antoine de Pardaillan de Gondrin, Duc d'Antin (1708â1719, Versailles, MusÃ©e National du ChÃ¢teau, inv. 7560).

description_block:
Son of Gaspard de Rochechouart de Mortemart and Louise de Maure, Gabriel de Rochechouart spent most of his childhood playing games with the Dauphin, Louis XIII. This friendship led to him receiving many favours from the King, once he was freed from his motherâs tutelage. In 1630, the sovereign appointed him First Gentleman of the Kingâs Chamber with a pension of 6,000 livres. He was made Knight of the Kingâs Orders in 1633 and accompanied the King on his many military expeditions. Gaspard de Rochechouart skilfully managed his career at court without ever getting involved in the various conspiracies that were hatched against Cardinal Richelieu at that time. He deployed the same prudence and diplomacy under the regency of Anne of Austria and at the time of the Fronde rebellion. In 1650, he was promoted to the title of Duc et Pair de France, retaining his position as First Gentleman of the Kingâs Chamber under the new sovereign Louis XIV.
Louis XIV appointed him Governor of Paris and the Ãle-de-France in 1669, enabling him to offer his children prestigious positions at court. In 1632, he married Diane de Grandseigne, lady in waiting to the queen, Anne of Austria. They had five children, four of whom became famous. Their son, Louis-Victor de Rochechouart, Duc de Mortemart then de Vivonne, a childhood friend of Louis XIV, became MarÃ©chal de France. FranÃ§oise-AthÃ©naÃ¯s de Rochechouart de Mortemart, the future Marquise de Montespan, the best known of Louis XIVâs mistresses, gave the sovereign seven illegitimate children. Marie-Madeleine de Rochechouart, known as âthe pearl of abbessesâ, was appointed Abbess of Fontevraud, a role previously reserved for princesses.

Strictly educated, he became interested in art and before long became a significant collector, chiefly of porcelain, gemstones and paintings. At the age of nineteen, Louis de France married Maria Anna of Bavaria with whom he had three children: Louis, Duc de Bourgogne; Philippe, Duc dâAnjou and future King of Spain; and Charles, Duc de Berry. A widower at the age of twenty-eight, his second marriage was to Emilie de Joly de Choin, who had been his mistress for years. Louis died before his father in 1711, so never ascended the throne. He was named Grand Dauphin after his death, so as to avoid confusion with his son Louis, Duc de Bourgogne. The Grand Dauphin is shown here wearing armour that alludes to his military might, with the ribbon of the Order of the Holy Spirit across his breast. His facial features are youthful and aristocratic. The author of our painting could have been inspired by Pierre Drevetâs engraving, in reverse, produced in 1700 or 1701 after a painting by Hyacinthe Rigaud in which Louis de France is portrayed waist-length, or alternatively by Robert Gaillardâs engraving, facing the same way but with the later date of 1711.

Daughter of Gabriel de Rochechouart, Marie-Madeleine de Rochechouart was appointed abbess of Fontevraud Abbey by the king in 1670. She was included by Gilles MÃ©nage in his list of women philosophers and was well versed in scholastic theology, maintaining correspondence with Charles Testu.She came to court during the final years of her sister AthÃ©naÃ¯s de Montespanâs favour and became acquainted with Madame de Scarron, with whom she maintained a friendly correspondence. She died at Fontevraud Abbey surrounded by works of morality, piety, and literary criticism. Louis de Rouvroy, duc de Saint-Simon claimed that her beauty eclipsed that of Madame de Montespan.
Initially accommodating men and women in the same buildings, the Abbey of Fontevraud eventually grew into a double monastery, in the spirit of Gregorian reform. It began to decline in the thirteenth century but was later run for nearly two centuries by abbesses from the Bourbon family. In 1738, Louis XV entrusted the education of his four youngest daughters to the Fontevraud nuns, which necessitated the building of a new residence, the Logis Bourbon.

Ludwig Braun was a German history and battle painter, who was born in 1836 in SchwÃ¤bisch Hall and died in 1916 in Munich. After studying at the Technical University in Munich and the arts school in Stuttgart, he illustrated the War of the Duchies in 1864 and then accompanied the German army during the war of 1870â71. He was particularly well known for his panoramas of battle scenes, a format that was very popular in the nineteenth century.
In this painting, the troops of Baron Hunolstein and his cousin Dietrich von Daun face each other in a battle of 1360, probably in the context of the Hundred Years War (1337-1453). This year was also marked by the signing of the Treaty of BrÃ©tigny by John II of France and Edward III of England, which brought about a truce of nearly nine years. The arms of the Hudolstein family are visible in the upper right of the painting: red and white, they are also those of the husband of Marie-ThÃ©rÃ¨se de Martainville, seen on the marital coats of arms in the right corner of their portrait (see lot 137). The castle that dominates the background could be Burg Eltz, a highly strategic military stronghold belonging to the Hunolstein baronetcy.

The original composition, begun in 1748, was only completed in 1754, after the modelâs death. It was exhibited at the Salon the following year, where it met with resounding success. There are many known replicas by Nattier, his workshop and his circle, some with variations, a number of which are also in the ChÃ¢teau de Versailles (see for example inv. description_block:
In an article published in April 2022, Martin Eidelberg attributed this Peasant dance as âwithout doubt executed in the style of Quillardâ, despite the fact that it had been sold several times as an autograph work by Jean-Baptiste Pater (âExpanding Quillardâs Åuvreâ, watteauandhiscircle.org). It does indeed appear that the signature was added later. The original version of the composition is in the National Gallery of Ireland in Dublin assigned to Pierre-Antoine Quillard (Wedding Festivities, inv. NGI. 564), while a second variant was sold on the Paris art market in the 1950s (M. Eidelberg, âAutour du nom de Quillardâ, in Bulletin de la SociÃ©tÃ© de lâhistoire de lâart franÃ§ais, 1979, p. 133). The pose of the central couple is an emblematic element of this artistâs work, repeated in many of his paintings, with a particular fondness for the male figure with his chin tilted upwards. As with all of Watteauâs disciples, the paintingâs colours are influenced by the Venetian School and Rubens. This type of image also owes much to Netherlandish genre painting, relying on iconographical codes established by artists such as David Teniers. His village celebrations include singing, dancing, musicians and feasts shared by adults and children in a joyfully tumultuous vein; the idea has been revisited here, but adapted to the aesthetic norms of the eighteenth century (M. Eidelberg, Watteau et la fÃªte galante, exh. cat., Valenciennes, 2004, p. 216).
Pierre-Antoine Quillard was probably one of the assistants in Watteauâs studio in about 1712â1715. He went to Portugal as a natural history illustrator and here found the recognition that had eluded him in his homeland. He became painter to John V of Portugal in 1727 and worked for the Portuguese aristocracy. He continued to produce fÃªtes galantes and pastoral scenes, as well as large altarpieces and official court portraits (M. Eidelberg, 2004, op. cit., p. 278). His career was tragically ended by illness, and much of his work was destroyed in an earthquake in Lisbon in 1755.

description_block:
This portrait attributed to the workshop of Martin van Meytens the Younger seems to be a partial reproduction of the figure of Joseph in the portrait of the three eldest sons of Maria Theresa of Austria and Francis I, displayed in the Royal Palace in Vienna, on the north wall of the Balcony Room. Elected Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire after the death of his father in 1765, Joseph II also became co-regent of the Habsburg estates with his mother, before inheriting them when she died in 1780. He introduced reforming policies, sometimes taken to extremes, in his efforts to transform the government from top to bottom. These brutal changes sparked the populationâs discontent, even resulting in uprisings such as the Brabant Revolution in 1789.
The young prince is shown in the military uniform of an officer, with long gold aiguillettes falling from his right shoulder and a tricorn hat tucked under his left arm. His status is apparent in his red suit, richly embroidered with motifs in gold thread, and the fine lace cuffs emerging from his sleeves. The insignia of the Order of the Toison dâOr hangs from a red ribbon to rest on his breast. This same composition is revisited by Van Meytens in the family portrait of Francis I and Maria Theresa, painted in about 1755 and now in the ChÃ¢teau de Versailles (inv. MV 3860).

description_block:
Etienne Jeaurat (1699â1789), the French painter and draughtsman, was trained by Nicolas Vleughels, who took him to Rome in 1724 when he was appointed director of the AcadÃ©mie de France there. Upon his return, Jeaurat was approved by the AcadÃ©mie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture in 1731 and admitted in 1733. He became in turn professor, rector and chancellor, then Painter to the King and finally, in 1767, Keeper of the Kingâs Paintings.He exhibited regularly at the Salon and became famous for his genre painting, with humorous and even satirical illustrations of his contemporariesâ lives, both ordinary people and the bourgeoisie. Jeaurat made his mark on eighteenth century art with his choice of subjects and his realistic view of society, in contrast to the Rococo style that was then dominant. While the artists of the court favoured mythological and religious themes or portraits, Jeaurat, despite being trained as a history painter, concentrated on the depiction of ordinary life under Louis XV: street scenes, the countryside, fÃªtes, domestic or shop interiors. His works were widely circulated as engravings.
At the 1763 Salon, Jeaurat exhibited Javotteâs Lemons, a scene inspired by one of Jean-Joseph VadÃ©eâs stories, published in 1758, showing that the popular â even vulgar â literature typical of VadÃ©eâs writing could inspire artists of the eighteenth century. In fact, the author was even portrayed by Jeaurat in one of his compositions: The Poet Piron Dining with his Friends VadÃ© and CollÃ© (oil on canvas, 54.5 x 66.5 cm, MusÃ©e du Louvre, Paris, inv. RF 2440).
The scene takes place inside an inn, where four male figures are gathered around a laid table. A fifth has risen from the table and is seen from the back on the far right. To the left of the composition, a man is picking up oyster shells scattered across the floor. Two female figures are approaching the table. One has come from the kitchen, holding a bottle in one hand and a tray with a glass in the other. The second woman is presenting the seated men with a wicker tray containing lemons, while one of the diners grasps her left wrist. The paintingâs title is inscribed on a pilaster in the background, above some caricatural graffiti and beneath a figurative medallion.Not much admired by Diderot, as evidenced in his Salon de 1763, the painting was however noted by Mathon de la Cour, who remarked in his Lettres Ã  Madame ***, sur les peintures, les sculptures et les gravures exposÃ©es dans le salon du Louvre en 1763: âLe public lâa vu avec quelque plaisir.â (âthe public viewed it [the painting] with some pleasureâ). The work appealed to the Marquise de Pompadour, who preferred this scene to the painting The Graces Enchained by Van Loo (see S. Puychevrier, Etienne Jeaurat: essai historique et biographique sur cet artiste, Paris, 1862, p. 15).
There is a known preparatory study for this painting, in black chalk and wash highlighted with white gouache, now in the Metropolitan Museum, with the title Three Men at a Table (New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art, inv. 1999.150; ill. 1).

Although he had tried out almost all painting genres, Philippe-Jacques de Loutherbourg (1740â1812) is chiefly known as a painter of landscapes and marine scenes, fields in which he excelled, bringing him prestige at a very young age. Approved and then accepted into the AcadÃ©mie de Peinture et de Sculpture in Paris in 1767, he exhibited a very large number of paintings at the Salons du Louvre between 1763 and 1771, the year he moved to London.
The present painting, which depicts a picturesque landscape inspired by the Lake District, which Loutherbourg had visited in the 1780s, is entirely typical of the works he painted in his English period. This composition reprises a portrait of Marie-Antoinette painted by Alexander Kucharski between 1789 and 1790. The original painting, which had as a pendant a portrait of King Louis XVI, belonged to the Comte de Provence (the future King Louis XVIII), who kept it in his study in the Tuileries (Sotheby's sale, Monaco, 20â21 June 1987, lot 407). Although already well integrated into the French aristocracy, Kucharski succeeded Elisabeth VigÃ©e-Le Brun as Marie-Antoinetteâs painter when she was exiled in 1789. He made many portraits of the queen and the dauphin, in oil, in pastel and in miniature. Neil Jeffares has also identified a gouache identically replicating the present portrait of Queen Marie-Antoinette (see N. Jeffares, Dictionary of pastellists before 1800, online edition no. J.438.168).
Her face turned to the left, Marie-Antoinette holds herself proudly, wearing a satin dress under the royal cloak trimmed with ermine. Later, Kucharski would paint the queen in mourning, at the Temple prison.

description_block: GÃ©rardâs Homer was conceived as the pendant to Belisarius, a painting made a few years earlier. The complete composition is now only known to us from an engraving: anticipated at the Salon in 1814, in the end the painting was never revealed to the public: the artist himself refused to show it and went as far as destroying it a few years later â but only partially, according to a suggestion made by Alain Latreille... Several contemporary descriptions nevertheless evoke an exceptional painting: Charles-Paul Landon devoted a whole article to it in his review of the 1814 Salon, expressing regret that the artist had âdeprived the public of the sight of this new workâ (C.-P. Landon, Annales du MusÃ©e et de l'Ã©cole moderne des beaux-arts. Salon de 1814, Paris, 1814, pp. 91â92, pl. 65). He reproduced the engraving of it. The date that the work was destroyed remains uncertain: Michelet saw it when he visited the Galerie Leuchtenberg in 1842 and described it in his Journal; while in 1856, Henri GÃ©rard, the artistâs nephew, declared that the painting had been âdestroyed by its authorâ (H. GÃ©rard, Åuvre du baron FrancÌ§ois GeÌrard, 1789-1836: tableaux Part II, Paris, 1856, no pagination). Alain Latreille suggests that our painting is the sole remaining fragment of the composition, GÃ©rard having chosen to preserve only the figure of Euplocamie, the most admired and original element of the painting. In the traditional version of Herodotusâs account, it was Glaucus who came to the aid of Homer, rather than his daughter. According to Herodotus, when Homer learned that Thestorides had stolen his poems, he left by boat for Chios. After the fishermen who conveyed him there left him on the shore, the blind Homer wandered around the island until he was attacked by dogs guarding a flock of sheep. It was then that Glaucus came to his rescue. Baron GÃ©rard chose instead a more contemporary version of the episode by Louis-NÃ©pomucÃ¨ne Lemercier, narrated in his poem HomÃ¨re, Alexandre, published in 1800, which substituted Euplocamie for her father. GÃ©rard thus hoped to emphasize the contrast between the figure of old age represented by Homer and that of youth embodied by Euplocamie. It was this contrast which, in the artistâs lifetime, was most admired. It seems entirely consistent that GÃ©rard, while dissatisfied with his composition in general, would nevertheless have wished to preserve this fragment which he too must have thought a worthy example of his work.

description_block: LÃ©on Riesener (1808â1878) was a pupil of Baron Antoine-Jean Gros (1771â1835) and the grandson of Jean Henri Riesener, the great cabinet maker of the Louis XVI period. LÃ©on Riesener is especially known for his famous portrait of EugÃ¨ne Delacroix in the Louvre (inv. no. RF 1960-58). He was first cousin to Delacroix, who was ten years older than him. The two men were close and painted together in Normandy in 1823. They shared their opinions on painting and agreed on many subjects, particularly questions of colour, which they regarded as the essential and primary aspect of their trade. Delacroix bought the painting AngÃ©lique from his cousin; it is now in the Louvre (inv. no. RF 1970 37). Riesener started exhibiting at the Salon in 1830. His first works were naturalist subjects and he received his first commission from the state in 1839; this was followed by several others, notably the decorations for the library in the Chambre des Pairs and for the Ministry of the Interior. From 1857 onwards, Riesener often travelled to Beuzeval near Houlgate where he had bought a mill, principally to pursue his research into colour, working from life and from the nature around him. He was regularly joined there by his friends Constant Troyon and Paul Huet. This spectacular pastel, the artistâs favourite medium alongside oil painting, demonstrates both Riesenerâs talent as a portrait painter and his particular interest in colour. The treatment of the flesh tones, the various materials, the modelâs dress and the horse as well the natural setting are striking both for the artistâs dexterity and for the subtle colours. Several Impressionists, including Renoir, paid tribute to him on his death in 1878, recognising that his work and especially his research into colour seemed to have paved the way for the next generation.

Originally from Nantes, Luc-Olivier Merson joined Pilsâs studio in Paris; awarded the Prix de Rome in 1869, he undertook a long journey through Italy, where he discovered the works of the great masters of the Renaissance. When he returned to France, he settled on the banks of the Loire and focused on historical, mythological, military and religious subjects.
Initially exhibiting at the Paris Salon, from 1885 onwards Merson preferred the provincial Salons, more suitable for his small-scale works of religious subjects. Lâangelo pittore is among the last works he sent to Paris, for the 1884 exhibition; it subsequently appeared in the Salons in Nantes and then Bordeaux, where it seems to have found a buyer. Its location had been unknown since 1892, and is described accordingly in the catalogue for the exhibition devoted to the artist at the MusÃ©e des Beaux-Arts in Rennes (see Literature).
Merson here depicts the legend of the painting angel who took advantage of Fra Angelico falling asleep to borrow his brushes and complete the face of the Virgin in the fresco of the vault of the Basilica di San Marco in Florence. The evocation of a dreamlike world associated with an angelic vision is very typical of Mersonâs oeuvre.

Along with Axeli Gallen-KallelÃ  and Helen Schjerfbeck, Albert Edelfelt was one of the three most important Finnish painters of the late nineteenth century, the golden age for pictorial art in the country, which was then still under Russian rule.
Born into an aristocratic Swedish-speaking family, Edelfelt briefly attended the University of Helsinki before beginning his artistic training at the AcadÃ©mie des Beaux-Arts in Antwerp, which he soon left in order to settle in Paris in 1874. Turning away from history painting and influenced by his friends, the French artists Dagnan-Bouveret and Bastien-Lepage, he moved towards a naturalism that led him to depict scenes of everyday life, both in Paris and during his frequent return visits to his homeland, where his radical new art soon established him as one of the major painters of the new generation.He began work on the Portrait of Madame de Saussine in Paris in late June/ early July 1885 and finished it.
The creation of the painted portrait was preceded by a detailed preparatory drawing, focusing on the old womanâs features, which is now in the Ateneum in Helsinki (inv. A II 1321; ill. 1). An examination of the original canvas, which is in perfect condition, reveals that Edelfelt decided to change the format while he was working on the painting. Having begun with a squarer format, which he may have felt constricted his model within an overly tight composition, the artist added a band of canvas about 14 cm wide on the left side, so as to fully represent the winter garden in which Madame de Saussine is peacefully seated.
1885, the year he painted this fine portrait, was a crucial year for Edelfelt in France: it was then that he achieved public recognition thanks to the huge success of his Portrait of Pasteur, which dated to this period. It remains to this day by far the most famous image of the French scientist (Paris, MusÃ©e dâOrsay, inv. DO 1986 16; ill. 2).
